articles.title: Why the T-90 Needs a Third Layer: Drone-vs-Drone Interceptors for the Fiber-Optic Threat
articles.text:
The Indian Army’s T-90 Bhishma fleet is the armoured spearhead of any future thrust along the western and northern borders. Over 1,600 are in service, with hundreds more on order, and the latest T-90 Bhishma Mk III incorporates indigenous thermal sights, digital ballistic computers and more powerful 1,350 HP engines. Yet for all this modernisation, the fleet carries a structural vulnerability that no amount of composite armour or explosive reactive armour (ERA) can close: the sky above the turret.
The Russia-Ukraine war has made the case with brutal clarity. Russia is estimated to have lost roughly 3,000 tanks and 9,000 armoured vehicles in a single year to drones, artillery and anti-tank guided missiles . FPV quadcopters costing a few hundred dollars have repeatedly destroyed heavily armoured main battle tanks by striking the turret roof, engine deck, optics and ammunition stowage — areas where passive protection is thinnest. India’s T-90s rely on Kontakt-5 ERA and composite armour with no hard-kill Active Protection System (APS) currently fitted, leaving them exposed to exactly the same top-attack and loitering-munition threat that has devastated armoured formations in Ukraine
The Army recognises the problem and has moved to address it. The question is whether the current roadmap is sufficient — or whether the T-90 needs a dedicated third layer of protection that neither soft-kill electronic warfare nor conventional hard-kill APS can provide.
The Threat That Defeat EW
To understand why a third layer is needed, it is necessary to understand what the first two layers cannot stop.
Fiber-optic-guided FPV drones have emerged as the single most disruptive tactical innovation of the Ukraine war. Instead of using a radio-frequency control link, these drones spool out a thin glass fiber-optic cable — thinner than fishing line, approximately 0.25 mm in diameter — as they fly. The cable carries control commands from the operator and high-definition video back, at the speed of light, with zero latency and zero electromagnetic signature .
The implications for electronic warfare are profound. No RF jammer, regardless of power or sophistication, can affect a fiber-optic drone in flight. The drone emits nothing, so passive RF detection cannot locate the operator. GPS spoofing is irrelevant because the video link is the primary navigation aid. Russia’s sophisticated EW suite — Krasukha-4, Murmansk-BN, Pole-21, Zhitel — systems that cost hundreds of millions of dollars, are simply bypassed The cable breaks on impact, so the drone does not drag the wire into the target. Reports indicate that approximately 80 percent of certain hostile drones now rely on fiber-optic guidance.
The upgrade cost is approximately $60 — a spool of cable, a dual-channel control module and a modified ground station . Against a $2-3 million tank, paying $3,000 instead of $500 per drone is a trivial exchange . There is also a newer complication. The latest FPV strike drones increasingly incorporate onboard AI machine-vision modules — such as Ukraine’s TFL-1, costing $150-$620 — that allow the drone to autonomously track and engage targets in the final 500 metres, the exact zone where vehicle-mounted jammers typically sever RF control links. This fire-and-forget capability boosts strike success rates two to five times while raising per-unit cost by only 10-20 percent.
For Indian planners, the threat is not theoretical. Pakistan and China both have access to commercial drone technology and the fibre-optic guidance concept is simple enough that any country with a fiber-optic cable manufacturer can replicate it . The cable is commercially available. The $60 module requires no classified technology.
What the Army Is Already Doing
The Indian Army’s response has been multi-pronged but, critically, does not yet close the fiber-optic gap.
Soft-kill and hard-kill APS: In February 2025, the Army issued a Request for Information (RFI) for a modular indigenous APS for the T-90 fleet. The system is required to combine soft-kill measures — laser warning receivers, electronic jammers, smoke grenades — with hard-kill interceptors, and must include Counter-UAS capability to detect FPV drones, swarm drones, loitering UAVs and kamikaze drones . A separate RFI followed in April 2025 for 75 platform-based C-UAS systems for both T-90 and T-72 tanks, with hard-kill cues feeding the existing anti-aircraft machine guns.
DRDO is developing an indigenous hard-kill APS through CVRDE and HEMRL, with interceptor capability against threats travelling over 1,500 m/s and top-attack coverage The system was first showcased at Aero India 2025, featuring four X-band radar panels providing 360-degree coverage and turret-mounted interceptors. L&T has also signed an MoU with Rafael to locally manufacture the combat-proven Trophy APS, which received a dedicated drone-defence upgrade in October 2024 ].
Directed energy: The Army is examining a 10 kW laser shield concept where select “shield tanks” within a formation of 20-40 vehicles would carry laser systems and automated CIWS to create a protective bubble
Indigenous C-UAS systems: The Army has issued Project Sanction Orders for the Bhargavastra counter-drone system, developed by Economic Explosives Limited (EEL). Bhargavastra employs a layered kinetic architecture with up to 64 micro-rockets or micro-missiles in a single salvo, with unguided rockets for dense formations and precision-guided micro-missiles for individual targets at ranges up to 2.5 km The system is vehicle-mounted on a 7.5-ton 4×4 platform .
The Gap: Why Current Layers Are Necessary but Not Sufficient
Each layer the Army is pursuing addresses part of the threat, but none closes the fiber-optic drone gap decisively.
Soft-kill EW is the foundation of any C-UAS architecture, but it is structurally ineffective against fiber-optic drones. By definition, there is no RF signal to jam, no GPS to spoof and no electromagnetic emission to detect [cite:9b2af009]. The soft-kill layer will defeat standard RF-controlled FPV drones, but the most dangerous threat class — the unjammable fiber-optic variant — passes straight through.
Hard-kill APS like Trophy or the indigenous DRDO system is designed primarily to intercept anti-tank guided missiles, RPGs and HEAT rounds travelling at high velocities. While modern APS can engage larger loitering munitions, the engagement geometry against a small quadcopter approaching at 100-150 km/h from above is fundamentally different from intercepting a direct-fire missile. APS radars are optimised for larger, faster-crossing threats. Small, slow, low-flying drones present a different detection and tracking challenge. Magazine depth is also a concern — APS interceptors are finite and a coordinated swarm can exhaust them.
10 kW lasers are promising against small drones but face serious integration challenges on the T-90. Tanks were not designed to support high-energy directed weapons; the system requires stable power generation, thermal management, precise tracking and uninterrupted line-of-sight in dusty, vibrating, high-mobility conditions [cite:3ef1d0aa]. Power draw and heat dissipation remain unresolved engineering hurdles. Lasers are also degraded by dust, rain and fog — common conditions on Indian battlefields.
Bhargavastra is a capable area-defence system but is mounted on a separate 7.5-ton vehicle that operates alongside armoured formations rather than being organically integrated onto each tank [cite:7cdbde29]. In fast-moving mechanised operations, the reaction window for an FPV drone attack is measured in seconds. A separate C-UAS vehicle cannot protect every tank in a dispersed formation simultaneously.
The result is a gap: between the soft-kill layer that fiber-optic drones defeat by design, and the hard-kill/laser layers that struggle with the engagement geometry and magazine depth of small drone swarms, there is no organic, on-tank capability specifically optimised to kill drones that cannot be jammed.
The Third Layer: Drone-on-Drone Interception
The missing piece is a canister-launched interceptor-drone layer mounted directly on the T-90 — a “drone-vs-drone” capability that physically destroys incoming threats that defeat electronic warfare.
The concept is no longer theoretical. At Eurosatory 2026, Rafael and SpearUAV unveiled the Iron Wasp, a tube-launched interceptor drone designed to be mounted on armoured vehicles in canisters similar to smoke grenade launchers. The Iron Wasp uses AI-driven autonomous detection, tracking and engagement, with a kinetic hard-kill warhead of approximately 2 kg that physically destroys incoming drones. It is sensor-agnostic and integrates with Trophy, Drone Dome and remote weapon stations. Crucially, because it employs kinetic interception rather than electronic countermeasures, it can engage fiber-optic drones that no EW system can touch .
KNDS has demonstrated a similar “drone-interceptor-drone” concept under its TARGAS architecture at Eurosatory 2026, combining soft-kill effectors with a drone-interceptor-drone layer developed in collaboration with AERIX .
On the battlefield, the concept has already been validated in crude form. Russian forces have deployed the Elka interceptor — a fire-and-forget, X-winged drone with no explosive warhead that uses a reinforced spiked nose to shatter enemy drone airframes on impact. Launched from a pistol-like device, it autonomously homes in on a target up to 1.6 km away and cannot be jammed electronically during flight. Single airframes are estimated at $500 . Ukraine’s 3DTech is developing the “Khizhak Shooter,” an interceptor drone specifically designed to destroy enemy fiber-optic FPVs in flight .
The logic is compelling. Against a drone that defeats all electronic countermeasures, the only effective response is physical interception. An interceptor drone launched from the tank itself — carrying its own seeker, AI guidance and kinetic warhead — can engage threats that neither jammers nor APS radars are optimised to handle. The engagement cost is asymmetric in the defender’s favour: a $500-$1,000 interceptor destroying a $500 attacker is a sustainable exchange ratio, particularly when the alternative is losing a $3 million tank.
India’s Emerging Indigenous Interceptor Ecosystem
India’s defence startup ecosystem is already moving in this direction, though not yet at the scale or integration depth required for organic tank-mounted deployment.
VEDA Aeronautics (Delhi) is developing an autonomous high-speed interceptor drone employing a “hit-to-kill” engagement concept — the interceptor itself acts as the weapon, guiding itself into an incoming drone during the terminal phase without an explosive warhead. The platform has an operational range of approximately 5 km and 10 minutes endurance, with a modular design for integration with multiple radar and EO/IR sensor systems .
ASTRA Drones and Robotics Solutions (IIT Ropar-incubated) has unveiled the ASTRA Interceptor Drone, designed for rapid deployment against hostile UAVs and low-altitude aerial targets .
DRDO’s ULPGM-V3, a dual-mode UAV-launched precision-guided missile, has completed final trials in both air-to-ground and air-to-air modes, including interception of simulated aerial drones in counter-UAV roles . While currently designed for launch from MALE UAVs, the underlying guidance and seeker technology could inform a tank-launched interceptor variant.
These programs demonstrate that the domestic technological base exists. What is missing is the integration imperative — a doctrinal decision to mount interceptor-drone canisters on the T-90 as an organic layer within the APS architecture, rather than treating drone interception as a separate, vehicle-mounted area-defence mission.
What a T-90 Interceptor Layer Could Look Like
A practical architecture for the T-90 would combine four layers, each addressing a specific threat class:
Layer 1 — Soft-kill EW: RF jammers, laser dazzlers and multispectral smoke to defeat standard RF-controlled FPV drones and break ATGM guidance. This remains the first line of defence against the majority of drone threats but is structurally ineffective against fiber-optic and AI-autonomous variants.
Layer 2 — Hard-kill APS: Indigenous DRDO system or Trophy to intercept ATGMs, RPGs, HEAT rounds and larger loitering munitions kinetically. The Army’s RFI caps the system under 1,000 kg with 360-degree coverage and -6° to +20° elevation, tracking up to eight threats simultaneously and engaging four, even if they appear 0.4 seconds apart .
Layer 3 — Interceptor drones: Canister-launched kinetic interceptors (Iron Wasp-class or an indigenous equivalent from VEDA/ASTRA) specifically for fiber-optic and autonomous drones that defeat EW. Four to eight canisters mounted on the turret, each containing an AI-guided interceptor with its own seeker, would provide a magazine of reusable hard-kill engagements against the threat class that no other layer can reliably address. This is the missing layer.
Layer 4 — Directed energy (formation-level): 10 kW lasers on designated “shield tanks” within a formation, providing low-cost-per-shot engagement against large numbers of small drones at the group level.
The interceptor-drone layer is the bridge between the APS (which handles fast, direct-fire threats) and the formation-level laser shield (which handles volume). It is the only layer specifically designed for the drone that cannot be jammed.
Challenges and Honest Caveats
None of this is without difficulty. Canister integration on the T-90 turret must not compromise existing capabilities — the Army’s RFI explicitly states the APS must not denude existing tank functions or affect NBC protection and deep fording seals [cite:34b5339d]. Weight is a concern: every kilogram added to the turret affects the power-to-weight ratio, particularly at high altitude where the current 1,000 HP engine already experiences reduced performance .
Magazine depth remains the fundamental limitation of any finite-interceptor system. A coordinated swarm of 20 drones can exhaust a canister loadout, and reloading under fire is impractical. This is why the interceptor-drone layer cannot stand alone — it must operate within the layered architecture, with soft-kill handling the volume of standard RF drones, APS handling direct-fire threats and interceptors reserved for the fiber-optic and autonomous threats that nothing else can stop.
Detection and cueing are also critical. An interceptor drone can only engage what it can find. The T-90’s existing sensors are optimised for ground threats, not small UAVs approaching at low altitude. The interceptor layer would need to be integrated with the APS radar panels and dedicated EO/IR drone-detection sensors to provide timely cueing. Ukraine’s experience with the Khyzhak automated turret — which uses wide-angle and narrow-angle thermal cameras with a laser rangefinder and ballistic computer to detect and engage drones at up to 800 metres — demonstrates what is possible, but also that the sensor package is the hard part .
Finally, there is the question of whether the interceptor should be recoverable. Iron Wasp and the Elka are expendable — each engagement consumes one interceptor. A reusable interceptor that returns to the tank after a failed engagement would preserve magazine depth but adds enormous complexity in autonomous navigation and recovery. The expendable model is simpler and more realistic for initial deployment.
The Strategic Case
The strategic case for a third layer is not merely about protecting tanks. It is about preserving the offensive option.
India’s armoured doctrine envisions rapid mechanised thrusts across the plains of Punjab and the deserts of Rajasthan, with T-90 formations acting as the spearhead. If an adversary can saturate the airspace above an armoured column with fiber-optic drones that no EW system can defeat, the entire concept of deep armoured penetration comes into question. Tanks that cannot move without being destroyed from above are tanks that cannot perform their offensive function.
The problem is particularly acute in India’s specific terrain. Punjab’s canal-and-river network forces armoured columns through predictable choke points — bridges and crossing sites where fiber-optic drones, immune to jamming, can create high-attrition killing zones ]. In Ladakh and Arunachal, where the Zorawar light tank is being inducted specifically for high-altitude warfare, the same drone threat applies in even more restrictive terrain.
The Zorawar programme has already recognised this: the first 59 tanks will be equipped with Trophy APS, and the indigenous APS under development is a hybrid soft-kill/hard-kill system explicitly designed to counter drone swarms and loitering munitions in mountainous terrain. But the Zorawar is a 25-tonne platform designed from scratch with APS integration in mind. The T-90 is a legacy platform that must be retrofitted, making the integration challenge harder and the case for a modular, canister-based interceptor layer stronger — because it can be added without redesigning the vehicle.
The Indian Army’s current roadmap — soft-kill EW, hard-kill APS, Bhargavastra area defence and the exploratory laser shield — is necessary and broadly correct in direction. But it is not sufficient against the specific threat that has emerged as the defining challenge of modern armoured warfare: the fiber-optic drone that defeats every electronic countermeasure by design.
A canister-launched interceptor-drone layer on the T-90, integrated with the APS radar and EO/IR sensors, is the missing piece. It is technologically feasible — the Iron Wasp, Elka and indigenous VEDA/ASTRA programs demonstrate the building blocks exist. It is doctrinally necessary — no other layer can reliably engage an unjammable drone approaching at 100+ km/h. And it is economically rational — the cost of an interceptor drone is a fraction of the cost of the tank it protects.
The fiber-optic threat has shifted the contest from the electromagnetic domain, where India’s EW investments hold value, to the physical domain, where only kinetic interception works. The T-90 was designed for a battlefield where the primary threat came from the ground. The third layer would prepare it for a battlefield where the most dangerous threat comes from above — and cannot be jammed.

articles.title: Why India’s Single-Crystal Turbine Blades Are a Generation (or Three) Behind the World’s Aerospace Leaders
articles.text:
India has made genuine, hard-won progress in one of aerospace engineering’s most demanding disciplines: casting single-crystal turbine blades for jet engines. But mastering the basic process is only the entry ticket to a field where the world’s leading aerospace powers, the United States, France, Japan, and the United Kingdom among them, are operating multiple technological generations ahead. Understanding that gap, and what it takes to close it, is central to India’s ambitions for genuine propulsion independence in programmes like Kaveri and AMCA.
What DRDO Has Actually Achieved
The foundation of India’s single-crystal capability rests with the Defence Metallurgical Research Laboratory (DMRL), a DRDO facility that successfully established a complete vacuum investment casting process for single-crystal high-pressure turbine blades. That achievement covers the full production chain, die design, wax pattern creation, ceramic mould formulation, casting, non-destructive evaluation, heat treatment, and precise dimensional measurement, applied to CMSX-4, a nickel-based superalloy widely used in Western aero-engines.
The technical hurdles DMRL had to clear along the way were genuinely significant. Engineers had to formulate a specialised ceramic mould composition strong enough to withstand the immense metallostatic pressure of molten CMSX-4 alloy at temperatures exceeding 1,500°C during casting, while also solving the precise thermal-gradient control needed to grow a defect-free single crystal structure rather than a conventional polycrystalline one. DMRL further developed a multi-step vacuum solutionising heat treatment schedule specifically tuned to CMSX-4’s complex chemistry, along with rigorous methods for verifying each blade’s crystallographic orientation. The lab has already supplied batches of these blades to HAL for indigenous helicopter engine applications, with production scaling toward several hundred units, and DRDO has since opened the machining stage of this process to private industry partners, extending the supply chain toward engines including Kaveri, the Tejas jet fuel starter, and the Adour engine powering the Jaguar fleet.
The Generational Ladder Nations Climb Through
Where India’s demonstrated capability currently sits becomes clearer against the broader generational framework used to classify single-crystal superalloys, a classification built around alloy composition, achievable temperature tolerance, and the inclusion of costly refractory elements like rhenium and ruthenium.
First- and second-generation single-crystal alloys, generally understood to represent India’s current baseline, use lower to moderate rhenium content, typically around 3 percent. Their defining achievement is eliminating grain boundaries entirely within the blade structure, which sharply reduces high-temperature creep and allows turbine entry temperatures to reach roughly 1,400°C to 1,450°C. Third- and fourth-generation alloys push further, incorporating higher rhenium concentrations of 5 to 6 percent alongside ruthenium and other elements that meaningfully boost creep strength and phase stability at elevated temperatures. Fifth- and sixth-generation alloys, the domain of programmes led by organisations like Japan’s IHI Corporation and America’s GE Aerospace and Pratt & Whitney, employ dense concentrations of ruthenium and further-optimised refractory metal chemistry, enabling metal surface temperatures to endure past 1,100°C to 1,200°C even before internal air cooling is factored in, which in turn allows overall turbine entry temperatures to exceed 1,600°C to 1,700°C.
Why the Generational Gap Actually Matters
This isn’t an abstract materials-science distinction, it translates directly into fighter jet performance. Higher-generation blades allow an engine’s core to run at substantially higher temperatures, and in gas turbine thermodynamics, higher turbine entry temperature correlates directly with greater thrust-to-weight ratio and power density. That’s the difference between an engine that merely meets a thrust specification and one that gives a fighter genuinely superior acceleration, climb rate, and sustained manoeuvring performance.
Durability follows a similar pattern. Advanced fifth- and sixth-generation microstructures are specifically engineered to resist “rafting,” the gradual, microscopic degradation of internal crystal phases that occurs under sustained centrifugal and thermal loading across thousands of tactical flight hours. A blade that rafts prematurely doesn’t just underperform, it shortens the entire engine’s usable service life and drives up long-term maintenance costs.
The Real Bottleneck Isn’t Casting, It’s Everything After
Perhaps the most important insight in understanding this gap is that knowing how to cast a first-generation single-crystal blade in a vacuum furnace, which DMRL has genuinely mastered, is only the entry barrier to the field, not the finish line. The far harder, more jealously guarded intellectual property lies in formulating the precise multi-step vacuum heat treatments, proprietary ceramic shell compositions capable of surviving extreme metallostatic pressures without cracking, and exact thermal-gradient control regimes needed for fifth- and sixth-generation alloy compositions specifically. These are not published formulas, they represent decades of accumulated, closely held process knowledge inside a handful of companies and national laboratories worldwide, exactly the kind of tacit engineering expertise that can’t simply be reverse-engineered from a finished blade or purchased off a shelf.
What This Means for Kaveri and AMCA
For India’s indigenous engine ambitions, this generational gap is arguably the single steepest technical barrier standing between current capability and genuine propulsion self-reliance. The original Kaveri programme’s struggles are a direct illustration of the stakes involved, the engine’s dry thrust output landed well below its target specification, with hot-section materials limitations cited as a significant contributing factor to that shortfall. Any future iteration of Kaveri, or the far more powerful indigenous engine envisioned for AMCA, will need turbine blade technology that has climbed meaningfully further up this generational ladder than DMRL’s current first/second-generation baseline, since the thrust, efficiency, and durability targets those programmes are chasing simply aren’t achievable on older-generation blade metallurgy.
The Bottom Line
DRDO’s single-crystal blade programme represents a genuine, hard-earned technical achievement, one that puts India among a still-small club of nations capable of producing this class of component domestically at all. But the honest assessment is that mastering the casting process was the easier half of the challenge. Closing the multi-generational gap in alloy chemistry, heat treatment, and ceramic mould engineering that separates India’s current capability from what the US, France, Japan, and the UK have spent decades refining will require sustained, patient materials-science investment, precisely the kind of unglamorous, long-horizon work that rarely makes headlines but ultimately determines whether India’s future fighter engines can compete on genuinely equal thermodynamic terms with the world’s best.

Indian Army Seeks Robotic 4×4 Mobility Platform to Rapidly Move and Relocate Field Artillery Guns
articles.text:
The Indian Army is reportedly seeking a dedicated mobility platform capable of rapidly deploying, towing and relocating field artillery guns, in a requirement that could point toward a new generation of remotely operated artillery-support vehicles.
According to reported specifications, the proposed platform would use a 4×4 cross-country configuration, have a towing capacity of approximately 4,000 kg, and incorporate a 10-kW electric motor. It is also reportedly required to achieve around 20 km of range under full load, a loaded speed of approximately 8–10 km/h and the ability to negotiate gradients of around 25 percent. The reported requirement also includes remote operation. These specifications remain subject to confirmation through an official Indian Army tender.
The most significant aspect of the requirement is not the towing capacity but the remote-operation feature. Rather than functioning as a conventional crewed artillery tractor, the platform appears intended to provide an unmanned or remotely operated means of moving guns between firing positions.
This could have a direct impact on artillery survivability.
Modern artillery warfare increasingly follows a shoot-and-scoot model. Once an artillery unit fires, the enemy can use counter-battery radars, electronic intelligence and unmanned aerial systems to identify the firing position and direct return fire. The longer a gun remains stationary after firing, the greater the opportunity for the adversary to engage it.
A dedicated mobility platform could therefore allow artillery crews to concentrate on firing while the towing vehicle rapidly moves the gun away from its firing position. If the vehicle can subsequently be controlled remotely, personnel do not necessarily have to remain exposed in the immediate vicinity of the gun during movement.
The requirement is particularly interesting because India’s artillery modernisation programme still includes a substantial number of towed artillery systems. The Indian Army operates systems including the M777 and is acquiring indigenous 155 mm artillery such as ATAGS. The ATAGS itself remains a towed 155 mm/52-calibre system, although its deployment can be supported by dedicated artillery tractors.
Traditional artillery tractors, however, require drivers and crews and are relatively large compared with the gun itself. India’s existing Field Artillery Tractor ecosystem includes platforms such as the Ashok Leyland FAT, which was developed specifically to tow artillery systems.
The reported new requirement suggests a different philosophy: make the mobility element smaller, remotely operated and potentially expendable compared with a conventional crewed tractor.
The 10-kW motor specification is also noteworthy. A relatively low-power electric drivetrain would be appropriate for a slow-moving platform whose primary task is towing rather than high-speed road movement. The reported 8–10 km/h loaded speed indicates that the vehicle is being optimised for tactical repositioning rather than long-distance transportation.
A 20 km range may also appear modest compared with conventional military vehicles, but the intended mission could explain the figure. The platform would not necessarily replace the army’s conventional artillery tractors. Instead, it could be used for short-distance movement between prepared firing positions, concealment areas and alternate gun positions.
The 4,000 kg towing requirement could cover a range of artillery systems, although the actual suitability would depend on the weight and terrain requirements of the selected guns. India’s modern 155 mm artillery systems can be considerably heavier than this, meaning the requirement may represent the towing load of a particular class of gun or equipment rather than the entire future artillery fleet.
The concept could eventually become particularly valuable for high-threat environments. An unmanned mobility platform could potentially move artillery through dangerous areas while reducing exposure of vehicle crews. It could also allow a gun detachment to reposition without requiring a conventional tractor to remain attached to the gun throughout the mission.
The requirement fits into a broader shift in military technology toward robotic logistics and unmanned ground systems. Instead of attempting to replace every crewed military vehicle, armies are increasingly examining whether specific high-risk or repetitive tasks can be performed by autonomous or remotely controlled platforms.

articles.title: General Atomics Eyes India for 155mm Long-Range Manoeuvring Projectile Capable of Striking Targets Beyond 120 km
articles.text:
US defence major General Atomics is preparing to offer its advanced 155mm Long Range Manoeuvring Projectile (LRMP) to India, potentially providing the Indian Army with a precision-guided artillery munition capable of engaging targets at ranges exceeding 120 kilometres.
The proposal comes as India continues to pursue long-range precision strike capabilities under its artillery modernisation programme, which seeks to extend the reach and lethality of existing 155mm gun systems.
Unlike conventional artillery shells that follow a purely ballistic trajectory, the LRMP is designed to manoeuvre during flight using aerodynamic control surfaces and onboard guidance. This enables the projectile to adjust its course after launch, increasing accuracy against stationary as well as selected time-sensitive targets while complicating enemy interception efforts.
General Atomics has developed the LRMP to be compatible with standard 155mm artillery systems, allowing armies to significantly increase the range of their existing guns without investing in entirely new launch platforms. The projectile combines extended-range propulsion with precision guidance to strike targets at distances of more than 120 km, nearly tripling the reach of many conventional artillery rounds.
For India, such a capability could complement indigenous long-range artillery programmes and enhance the operational effectiveness of platforms such as the Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System (ATAGS) and the M777 Ultra Light Howitzer, provided compatibility and integration requirements are met. A precision-guided projectile with a range exceeding 120 km would enable the Indian Army to engage high-value targets, command posts, logistics hubs and air defence assets from well behind the front lines.
The offer also aligns with India’s growing emphasis on long-range fires, driven by evolving operational requirements along both the western and northern borders. Modern conflicts have demonstrated the importance of precision artillery capable of delivering rapid, cost-effective strikes at extended distances, bridging the gap between conventional tube artillery and more expensive tactical missile systems.
General Atomics has been expanding its defence engagement with India across multiple domains. In addition to the MQ-9B High Altitude Long Endurance (HALE) unmanned aircraft programme, the company has expressed interest in collaborating with India on advanced technologies, including precision-guided munitions and autonomous systems.
If India decides to evaluate the LRMP, the projectile would likely compete alongside indigenous extended-range precision artillery ammunition currently under development by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Indian industry. Any future acquisition would also be expected to emphasise technology transfer, local manufacturing and integration with India’s domestic defence ecosystem under the government’s Make in India initiative.

articles.title: Rafale Local Production Could Extend Into the Early 2040s Even if Contract Is Signed This Year
articles.text:
If India concludes its long-awaited 114 Rafale contract by the end of this year, the programme is likely to unfold over more than a decade, with the final locally manufactured aircraft potentially rolling off the production line between 2038 and 2041, according to typical aerospace manufacturing timelines and defence acquisition practices.
While the first imported fighters could begin arriving around 2029, establishing domestic production for approximately 90 aircraft would require several years of industrial preparation before serial manufacturing reaches full capacity. The first phase of the programme would focus on establishing the manufacturing ecosystem in India. Even after the contract is signed, setting up a dedicated Final Assembly Line (FAL), transferring manufacturing documentation, qualifying suppliers and certifying production facilities typically requires two to three years.
During this period, the selected Indian production partner from a private-sector joint venture—would work with the foreign original equipment manufacturer (OEM) to establish assembly infrastructure, train personnel and validate manufacturing processes.
Initial production would likely begin with Semi Knocked Down (SKD) or Completely Knocked Down (CKD) kits imported from the OEM before progressively increasing indigenous content through localisation of components, structures and sub-systems. This gradual localisation approach has been followed in previous Indian aerospace programmes, including the Su-30MKI.
Once the production line reaches maturity, manufacturing rates would increase to steady-state output. Defence industry benchmarks indicate that advanced fighter assembly lines in India generally sustain production of around 8 to 12 aircraft annually, with peak output potentially reaching 12 to 16 aircraft per year under favourable supply-chain conditions.
Assuming approximately 90 aircraft are to be manufactured in India, a sustained production rate of 10 to 12 fighters annually would require roughly seven to nine years of continuous serial production.
Under this scenario, the first imported flyaway aircraft could enter IAF service around 2029, while the first Made-in-India serial-production fighter could emerge from the domestic assembly line around 2031 or 2032 after completion of technology transfer, tooling and production qualification activities.
At that point, domestic production would become the primary source of aircraft deliveries, with serial manufacturing continuing through the remainder of the decade.
Based on these production assumptions, the final locally manufactured aircraft would likely be delivered between 2039 and 2041, depending on annual production rates, localisation milestones and the stability of the global aerospace supply chain.
Such a timeline would make the MRFA programme one of India’s longest-running fighter manufacturing efforts, creating sustained work for the domestic aerospace industry over nearly a decade while enabling progressive transfer of manufacturing expertise and industrial capabilities.

Putting mice into hibernation causes a major loss of synapses
articles.text:
Our leading hypothesis for how our memories are stored is that when you learn something, the connections among neurons involved get stronger and physically larger, and that constitutes the memory. The trouble is that these connections significantly change over time—they’re plastic.

“If you compare the arrangement of these connections on day one with the same on day four or five, it's very, very different," says Kazumasa Tanaka, a neuroscientist at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Graduate University in Japan. To learn how a memory that can last for years can sit on hardware that shifts every few days, Tanaka’s team made the shift a bit more dramatic. In a recent Science study, they induced a hibernation-like state in mice, which basically erased the state of more than half of their synapses. And yet the mice apparently have kept their memories.

Hibernation on demand

Hibernation is a specialty of squirrels, hamsters, and bears, but the neural circuit that triggers it is conserved across mammals, and is present in species that never hibernate in the wild—like mice. In June 2020, a team of researchers led by Takeshi Sakurai, a neuroscientist at the University of Tsukuba and a collaborator on Tanaka’s study, developed a technique to artificially activate this hibernation circuit. This can be done by activating a population called Q neurons in a region of the hypothalamus.

articles.title: Dismantling the Roadless Rule threatens to disrupt wildlife and water in US
articles.text:
Pause for a moment and listen. What do you hear? Chances are, somewhere in the background, is the ever-present hum of a road.

More than 4.2 million miles of public roads crisscross the lower 48 states—enough to reach the Moon and back almost nine times. This vast network of roads spiderwebs its way across the contiguous US, leaving only about 5 percent as an inventoried roadless area or wilderness.

Now, some of those last remaining lands free of roads are under threat from the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of the 2001 Roadless Rule. That includes southeast Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, where eagles, bears, salmon, and many other species thrive in old-growth coastal forest along the Inside Passage.
